latest_nl_proof:
Assume that the rational function A(q)/B(q) is a polynomial in Z[q]. Then there exists a polynomial C(q) in Z[q] such that

A(q)=B(q)C(q).

Because A(q) and B(q) are both nonzero, C(q) must also be nonzero: if C(q)=0, then A(q)=B(q)C(q)=0, contradicting that A(q) is nonzero.

Now let r=deg(B) and s=deg(C). Since B and C are nonzero, we may write

B(q)=b_r q^r + b_{r-1} q^{r-1}+\cdots+b_0, with b_r\neq 0,
C(q)=c_s q^s + c_{s-1} q^{s-1}+\cdots+c_0, with c_s\neq 0.

In the product B(q)C(q), every term has degree at most r+s, because it comes from multiplying q^i by q^j with i\le r and j\le s. The coefficient of q^{r+s} is b_r c_s, which is nonzero because b_r and c_s are nonzero integers. Therefore the product B(q)C(q) has degree exactly r+s. Hence

deg(A)=deg(B(q)C(q))=r+s=deg(B)+deg(C).

Since C is a nonzero polynomial, deg(C)=s\ge 0. Therefore

deg(A)=deg(B)+deg(C)\ge deg(B).

This proves that deg(A)\ge deg(B).

quantifier_order: For all polynomials A and B with integer coefficients in q, assuming both are nonzero, if the quotient A divided by B is itself a polynomial with integer coefficients in q, then the degree of A is at least the degree of B.
